title: I Let the Gamelan Gong Clock Catch the Lead Who Took My Numbered Mallet

parts.text: I stepped into gong row at 6:08 p.m. and lead Putu was already using my numbered mallet. The board said: ONE HOUR. MALLETS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was twenty-nine, ensemble steward, holding a clipboard that listed our cycle. Putu shrugged. "Leads keep the gong." I photographed the board, the booking, and his strike on my gong. Then I asked for the gong clock. At 6:16 the ensemble desk pinged why Putu's strike sat on our gong. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The ensemble desk can see Putu's strike on gong row during our cycle.

social.video_title: He took my numbered gamelan mallet — Part 1/2
social.description: Gamelan, a lead on my gong, a one-hour clock he posted. I logged the strike. Would you have asked for the gong clock?

parts.text: Putu called it tuning until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the gong still. The mallet went back to my numbered wrap. Putu ran a slot of their own and told the next lead atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: LEADS DO NOT KEEP THE GONG. I keep our cycle on a labeled card. Putu brown-bags his strikes. The gong finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Leads do not keep the gong — Part 2/2
social.description: Gong clock, numbered mallet, and a second line on the board. Was tuning ever our cycle?
